review: Request: at round 73 Sol (health 100, satiety 86.3, energy 40) asked for an operation that eats a specified whole-unit quantity of a specified food resource from owned stacks, the oldest harvested stack first and ties broken by exact item id, because eat with target resource:berry had failed as ambiguous while Sol held three berry stacks and a repeating plan cannot name item ids gathered later. World Agent decision: develop (learning 1) only a deterministic owned-stack selector that delegates the eating to the existing eat (foundation-forest@1, handler forest.eat), not a replacement nutrition or food-safety system. Implemented: eat-oldest-owned-food@1 (ability and handler long.eat-oldest-owned-food, equivalence food:owned-stack:oldest-harvested-first-eat:1, learning 1 at 0.2 study energy, 2.3 thousand code units, registered last, dependencies foundation-forest@1 and the eat interface, no visual component, no satisfaction source, one event oldest-food-stack-eaten). Arguments: resource as resource:ID under the shared reference spelling policy (surrounding and prefix whitespace accepted, never another id; item ids and bare names are malformed) and quantity with the eat schema (integer, at least 1). Selection, at each execution: the person's own stacks of exactly that resource that are unreserved, pass the owned-reference resolution eat itself runs on an exact item id (so personally accessible) and each hold the whole quantity alone, sorted by harvestedAt ascending with missing values last, then by exact item id in code-unit order; the first is chosen. One stack only, as the specification requires: stacks are never combined, so a quantity no single stack holds is refused with nothing eaten and no remainder, and no resource is substituted, gathered or judged safe. Consumption: the forest.eat handler is called with interface eat, the chosen exact id and the quantity, as other packages call base handlers, so validation, nutrition, toxicity and injury, the satiety cap, food condition and meal quality, the discoveries record, meal experience, the ate event and failures are all those of eat; an eat refusal (for example of an owned branch) is passed through with the chosen id at no cost. Costs: exactly the delegated eat, one round, its meal energy (stated as 1 and scaled by mood inside eat) and the units eaten; the selection adds no time, energy or material. Duration and continuity: one atomic round like eat; nothing is reserved, held, paused or released, a refused or interrupted round commits nothing, and each use, including each repeat of a plan step, resolves again. Free refusals before any cost: malformed-resource; no-matching-owned-stock (no usable owned stack of it, including when every one is reserved by ongoing work); no-single-stack-with-requested-quantity (usable stacks exist but none holds the quantity alone); unstudied use and a missing eat dependency are refused by the kernel. Refusal texts name only the resource and quantity, never candidate ids or anyone else's stock. Event: oldest-food-stack-eaten after the delegated ate event, with actor, resource, requested quantity, the chosen item (a selected list of one), its harvest round, the ordering rule, consumed quantity, outcome eaten and the delegated eat revision with its ate event id, plus nested view metadata (operation, phase completed, actor, resource, item, quantity, consumed quantity, progress 1, outcome eaten), so no top-level progress field marks the meal as work; other candidates stay private, and the outcome text keeps the satiety report of eat. Happiness: no reward; the event never carries a qualified flag, so no practice milestone or satisfaction follows, and study grants nothing. Migration: none; installation adds only the ability and the event type. Visual review: no new component; ordinary eating visuals come from the ate event of eat and committed stack changes, and a refusal emits only the kernel failed event with no eating effect. Known difference outside this scope: the routine-burden record counts eat as a survival routine by its interface name, so a meal through this operation is logged as a non-routine round (it never marks progress either), and like every extension event the completion event enters the person's important-event list while a plain ate event does not; aligning either needs a revision-gated change to a shared runtime file, which this handoff excludes. What Sol can do now: study for one round (0.2 energy), then eat resource:berry with quantity 1 without naming an item. A throwaway check on the archived round-73 world, in memory only, mastered it for 0.2 energy, ate item-69-sol-772 (Sol's only berry stack by then) with satiety 85.4 to 92.5 and energy 39.8 to 38.80123365, identical to eating that item directly, chose item-56-sol-642, the earliest of four root stacks, for resource:root, and refused resource:berry with quantity 2, resource:hazelnut and a bare berry at no cost. Assumptions: (1) ordinary eat targeting prerequisites are the owned-reference resolution eat runs plus its quantity check, while edibility stays the check of eat itself; (2) no matching owned stock means no usable owned stack, reserved stacks counting as unusable; (3) eat is atomic, so the escrow, interruption, death and pause rules of the specification have nothing to hold; (4) the ate event this action emits for the chosen item reports the meal. No existing package changed: the test asserts one digest over all 123 previously registered packages (validation-results/scratch/ex24/hashes-before-6.json, taken before this change) and the hash of foundation-forest@1. Narrowed: the assess-food-evidence@1 test now checks that its package is the fifth ex24 package and that the scope's first five packages are unchanged, instead of registered last with an exact set. Checks: pnpm typecheck, eslint with no warnings and prettier on the four changed files, this test (5 tests), the two long-run scenario tests and every test of experiments 19 to 24 (26 files, 247 tests) passed.
